items.followUp: What observation in the Tyndall test distinguishes a colloid from a true solution?

rubric.why: The test requires passing light through the sample.
rubric.description: Describes passing a beam of light through the given solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the test.

accept: path of the beam becomes visible
rubric.why: Colloidal particles scatter light, making the beam's path visible.
rubric.description: States the observation and identifies it as evidence of a colloid.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the visible path due to scattering, with the conclusion that the sample is colloidal.

modelAnswer: Pass a beam of light through the given solution in a dark room.
If the path of the beam becomes visible due to scattering of light (the Tyndall effect), the sample is a colloidal solution.

items.followUp: Name one naturally occurring compound of sodium and one of calcium.

rubric.why: Both groups are reactive and occur naturally in combined form rather than as free elements.
rubric.description: States the general form in which alkali metals and alkaline earth metals occur in nature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that they are highly reactive and occur combined, not free.

rubric.why: The examples must represent both an alkali metal and an alkaline earth metal.
rubric.description: Gives a suitable compound example for each group.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct example from each group.

modelAnswer: Alkali metals and alkaline earth metals are highly reactive, so they occur in nature in the combined state, not as free elements.
Alkali metals occur in compounds such as sodium chloride and potassium chloride; alkaline earth metals occur in compounds such as calcium carbonate and magnesium carbonate.

items.followUp: How does the electropositive character of elements change down a group and across a period?

rubric.why: Electropositive character increases from top to bottom in a group.
rubric.description: Gives the trend in a group.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct direction.

rubric.why: Electropositive character decreases from left to right across a period.
rubric.description: Gives the trend across a period.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct direction.

modelAnswer: In a group, electropositive character increases from top to bottom.
Across a period, electropositive character decreases from left to right.

items.followUp: Write five properties of canal rays.

rubric.why: Straight-line travel is a characteristic property of cathode rays.
rubric.description: States that cathode rays travel in straight lines.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this property.

rubric.why: Cathode rays are negatively charged and are deflected toward a positive plate.
rubric.description: States their negative charge and response to an electric field.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this property.

accept: independent of the nature of the gas
independent of the material of the electrodes
rubric.why: Cathode-ray properties do not depend on the gas or electrode material used.
rubric.description: States that their properties are independent of the gas and electrodes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this property.

rubric.why: Cathode rays produce fluorescence when they strike certain substances.
rubric.description: States that cathode rays produce fluorescence.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this property.

rubric.why: Cathode rays possess energy and can produce mechanical effects or penetrate thin materials.
rubric.description: Gives one further property, such as possessing kinetic energy or penetrating thin metal foil.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one additional correct property.

modelAnswer: Cathode rays travel in straight lines.
They have a negative charge and are deflected toward the positive plate in an electric field.
Their properties are independent of the nature of the gas in the discharge tube and the material of the electrodes.
They produce fluorescence when they strike certain substances.
They possess kinetic energy; for example, they can rotate a light paddle wheel.

items.followUp: Write four properties of ionic compounds.

rubric.why: Covalent compounds generally have low melting and boiling points because the forces between their molecules are weak.
rubric.description: States that covalent compounds generally have low melting and boiling points.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this general property.

rubric.why: Covalent compounds generally lack mobile charged particles to carry an electric current.
rubric.description: States that covalent compounds generally do not conduct electricity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this general property.

rubric.why: Most covalent compounds are insoluble in water.
rubric.description: States their usual solubility in water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this general property.

rubric.why: Covalent compounds are generally soluble in organic solvents.
rubric.description: States their usual solubility in organic solvents.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this property.

rubric.why: Many covalent compounds are volatile or soft.
rubric.description: Gives one further suitable property.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that many covalent compounds are volatile or soft.

modelAnswer: Covalent compounds generally have low melting and boiling points because the forces between their molecules are weak.
They generally do not conduct electricity because they have no mobile ions or electrons.
Most are insoluble in water.
They are generally soluble in organic solvents.
Many covalent compounds are volatile or soft.

items.followUp: Define allotropy and explain why an element may show it, giving one example of a transition temperature.

rubric.why: Allotropy is the existence of different forms of the same element in the same physical state.
rubric.description: Defines allotropy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the essential definition.

rubric.why: Different arrangements of atoms in a crystal can give rise to different allotropic forms.
rubric.description: Gives a structural reason for allotropy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this reason.

rubric.why: Allotropic forms can differ in the number or arrangement of atoms in their molecules.
rubric.description: Gives a further valid reason for allotropy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for an additional reason.

rubric.why: Transition temperature is the temperature at which one allotropic form changes into another; sulphur changes form at about 96°C.
rubric.description: Defines transition temperature or gives the sulphur example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the definition or a correct example.

modelAnswer: Allotropy is the existence of an element in two or more different forms in the same physical state.
Allotropic forms may result from different arrangements of atoms in crystals.
They may also differ in the number of atoms in their molecules or in their molecular structures.
The temperature at which one allotropic form changes into another is called the transition temperature.
For example, rhombic sulphur changes into monoclinic sulphur at about 96°C.
